Jeevan, you asked how my sister Revathi and I made up. Okay. I'm Nitin. In March I promised Revathi I'd be at her graduation in Chennai, and I didn't go. A work thing, I told myself. Afterwards I did the usual: sent flowers, a big cake, a long message full of "you know how my boss is". She replied with one word: "Okay."

Then my mother said, "Flowers are not sorry." So I called Revathi and said it plainly. "I promised to come to your graduation and I didn't. That was wrong, and there's no excuse. I'm sorry." Then, which I had never done before: "What would help?"

She said, "Just show up next time." So now every family date goes into my calendar before any work meeting. In June I was there for her first day at the new job, with tea. She hugged me.

At the government school in Barwani, Ritu was captain of the kabaddi team, the loudest voice in class, the one who argued with the sports teacher about the new mats. Her friend Indu had never seen her lose an argument.

One Sunday Indu walked to Ritu's house to borrow a notebook. Ritu opened the door with her dupatta pulled low, said "Hmm, wait" in a voice Indu barely recognised, and went quietly back to rolling rotis beside her grandmother. When her uncle asked if she'd finished her studies, she said "Ji" and nothing more.

Walking Indu to the gate, Ritu whispered, "Don't tell anyone at school about this. And don't tell anyone here about the kabaddi captain thing."

"Why?" Indu asked.

Ritu shrugged. "It's simpler. Two Ritus, no fights." But her eyes looked tired.

Chetan's Nani died on Sunday night. His final exams began on Tuesday morning, the hostel generator had broken, and his train ticket home was for the day after the last paper, because Mummy had insisted: "Nani would want you to finish."

So he put it away. He studied by torchlight with Wasim. He wrote three papers in four days with a steady hand. When Wasim asked, "You okay?" he said, "Later. After the thermodynamics paper."

He did well; he could feel it. Wasim noticed he never once mentioned Nani, not even when his phone lit up with family photos.

The night after the last exam, on the train, Chetan finally opened the photo of Nani at his tenth birthday. He cried from Itarsi to Bhopal. Wasim, travelling with him, just passed tissues and said nothing.

qa.q: Why did Chetan keep saying "Later" when Wasim asked?
qa.a: Chetan was grieving but chose to put the sorrow aside to get through the exams, knowing he couldn't feel it fully and still write.

qa.q: What made Chetan's pause healthy rather than harmful?
qa.a: There was a later time to open it: on the train after the last paper he let the grief out, with Wasim beside him.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel sitting beside Chetan on the train?
qa.a: Wasim likely feels sad and protective, relieved Chetan is finally crying, and simply offers quiet company.

grounding: Shows a student who sets aside grief for his grandmother to get through exams, then lets it out on the train home.

When Shankar's Periappa died, it was the week of his semester exams at the Chennai college. He went to the funeral on Sunday, came back on the night bus, and on Monday morning he was in the exam hall, pen ready.

His roommate Deepak watched him study that week with a strange calm. Shankar made a timetable, stuck to it, ate on time, even ironed his shirt. Once Deepak saw him pick up the steel tiffin box Periappa had given him, pause, and put it away in the cupboard. "After the exams," Shankar said to nobody in particular.

He topped two papers. On the Saturday after the last one, he asked Deepak to come with him to the beach at Besant Nagar, where Periappa used to take him for sundal. They sat there till dark. Shankar talked about Periappa for two hours, and cried, and laughed.

qa.q: Where did Periappa use to take Shankar?
qa.a: Periappa used to take him to the beach at Besant Nagar for sundal.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when he put the tiffin box away?
qa.a: Shankar was grieving, and putting the box away was a way to set the sadness aside until after the exams.

qa.q: Why was the beach visit an important part of this?
qa.a: It was the later time to open the box; without it, the pause might have hardened into a wall.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt watching Shankar's calm during exam week?
qa.a: Deepak probably felt puzzled and a little worried by the strange calm, and relieved when they finally sat at the beach.

"Organic chemistry is on Thursday."
"Minakshi, Dadu's funeral was yesterday."
"I know." She didn't look up. "If I think about him now, I won't be able to stop. So I'm not thinking about him till Thursday afternoon."

Zubin was quiet. "Yeah. I'll bring the tea he liked. Too much cardamom."
She laughed, a little shakily. "Too much cardamom."
On Thursday afternoon they sat on the floor of Dadu's room with the letters and the tea. Minakshi read the first one aloud and didn't get past the second line.

You asked how married life is, Jyoti? Honest version. I'm Bhavna, and Pankaj is a wonderful salesman. I've seen him at the showroom: patient with every fussy customer, laughing at their jokes, remembering their kids' names.

Then he comes home at nine, and he's someone else. "Hmm." "Not now." "Can we not talk?" He eats looking at his phone. For the first few months I thought he'd stopped liking me.

Then one Sunday I watched him on a customer call from home. Warm, funny, forty minutes. When he hung up, he just sat there, empty, like a battery at one percent. That's when I understood. The kindness is real; it's just all spent before he reaches me.

So now we've agreed: for the first twenty minutes at home, he gets silence and tea. After that, we talk. It's better.

qa.q: What time does Pankaj come home?
qa.a: Pankaj comes home at nine.

qa.q: What did Bhavna feel in the first few months?
qa.a: Bhavna felt hurt and unsure, believing Pankaj had stopped liking Bhavna.

qa.q: Why does the twenty-minute arrangement help?
qa.a: It gives Pankaj time to recharge after spending his warmth on customers, so there is some left for real talk at home.

qa.q: What is the day like for Pankaj by nine o'clock?
qa.a: Pankaj is drained, like a battery at one percent, having spent his patience and charm on customers all day.

I'm Rukmini, and I've been married to Farida for two years. I visited her school once, on annual day. I watched her with a crying Class 3 boy: she knelt, spoke softly, and had him laughing within a minute. Parents lined up to thank her.

At home she's different. She comes in at six, drops her bag, and answers everything with "Mm." Last week I asked about her day and she said, "Please, no questions," quite sharply, and went to lie down with the lights off.

I don't know exactly what goes on inside her. But I notice that on holidays she's gentle again, and on Mondays she's the most tired. I think the patience is real; she just uses it all on those children.

So I've stopped asking at the door. I make tea, leave it by the bed, and wait. Around eight, she usually comes and finds me.

I'm Vidya, and last year I ran my life like a building with locked rooms. In one room was the credit card debt from my father's hospital bills, which I mentioned to no one, not even my sister Aditi. In another was my marriage, which was falling apart. At work I was the calm team lead who never talked about home.

It worked. I shipped every project. People called me unflappable.

Then one Tuesday my husband's lawyer emailed during a client call, and the card company phoned twice in the same hour. Both rooms burst open at once. I walked out of the meeting and cried in the stairwell.

Aditi was the one I called. She came that evening with dinner and a notebook. "Room by room," she said. We made a list. The next week I saw a debt counsellor, and I told my manager I needed some flexible days.

Uma
